title: Back-to-Back: UConn Repeats in Glendale
dek: UConn let Zach Edey score 37, took away Purdue's 3-pointers and won 75-60, becoming the first repeat national champion since Florida in 2006 and 2007.

setup.text: UConn arrived at the final 36-3 and the tournament's No. 1 overall seed, having won five NCAA games by 39, 17, 30, 25 and 14 points, the last an 86-72 semifinal over Alabama. One more win would make it the first repeat champion since Florida in 2006 and 2007.

Purdue, the Midwest's No. 1 seed, was one year removed from becoming only the second No. 1 seed ever to lose in the first round. It had 7-foot-4 Zach Edey, the AP Player of the Year and reigning Wooden Award winner, and the nation's second-best 3-point shooting team.

UConn's staff bet that Edey would get his points either way; he had averaged 24.9 in Purdue's wins and 25.0 in its losses. So the Huskies guarded him one-on-one with Donovan Clingan and spent their defensive attention on Purdue's guards and shooters.

story.text: Early on, the plan looked shaky. Edey had 14 points when his basket with about eight minutes left in the half put Purdue up 23-21, and he exchanged words with Hurley and the UConn bench.
Then the defense took hold. Edey made one field goal over the next 14:28 as UConn turned a two-point deficit into a nine-point lead, and Purdue attempted just two 3-pointers in the half.
Purdue's lone make from deep came from Braden Smith late in the half, and Hurley bolted onto the floor to call timeout. Stephon Castle's tip-in sent UConn to the locker room ahead 36-30.

sequence.text: Edey's jumper off a Smith pass gives him 14 points and Purdue the lead.
Clingan scores on a Tristen Newton feed and adds the free throw. Purdue never leads again.
Smith's 3 cuts the lead to two. It is Purdue's only 3-pointer of the night; UConn's timeout follows at 2:09.
Castle tips in Newton's miss for a six-point halftime lead.
Newton opens the second half with a 3, set up by Clingan.
Newton lobs to Samson Johnson for an alley-oop and UConn's first double-digit lead.
Newton slices through traffic for a lay-in.
After an Alex Karaban 3, Hassan Diarra's driving layup off a Newton pass makes it 56-40 and forces a Purdue timeout.
Cam Spencer's jumper in the paint builds the largest lead of the night, 18.
Edey scores his 37th point, the most ever by a player on the losing side of a title game.
Clingan's layup off a Karaban pass is the final basket. UConn is champion again.

quotes.text: We won — by a lot — again.
I just think it's the best two-year run in a very, very long time, just because of everything we lost from last year's team.
They just made a decision — we can defend the perimeter, and we can take this away from you.
The coaches made a point that we'd be really locked in if we could control their 3-point attempts.

aftermath.text: Newton, with 20 points, seven assists and five rebounds in the final, was named the Final Four's Most Outstanding Player; Clingan, Castle and Spencer joined him on the all-tournament team. UConn finished 37-3, a program record for wins.
Hurley became the first coach to win back-to-back titles since Billy Donovan did it at Florida in 2006 and 2007.
Two months later, on June 10, Hurley turned down a six-year, $70 million offer to coach the Los Angeles Lakers and stayed at UConn.
On Sept. 10, 2024, President Joe Biden welcomed the team to the White House to celebrate the title.

legacy.text: UConn joined Duke (1991-92) and Florida (2006-07) as the only repeat champions since UCLA's run under John Wooden.
ESPN Stats & Information found UConn was only the second program to win title games by 15 or more points in consecutive years, after UCLA's 1967-69 teams.
All six of UConn's championships came within 25 years, which tied it with North Carolina for the third-most in NCAA history.
